existing_observations.text: In Acts.10.21 aitia is used in its plain practical sense 'reason/cause' (for the men's coming) -- sitting within the base gloss with no notable divergence.

evidence.verse: And Peter went down to the men and said, “ I am the one you are looking for. What is the reason for your coming?”
When they had examined me, they wished to set me at liberty, because there was no reason for the death penalty in my case.
For this reason, therefore, I have asked to see you and speak with you, since it is because of the hope of Israel that I am wearing this chain.”
For this reason I remind you to fan into flame the gift of God, which is in you through the laying on of my hands,

senses.obs_text: In Act 10:21, Act 28:20 and 2Ti 1:6 the noun 'cause' is the ground on which something is done or asked: the cause of their coming, and 'for this reason' in Paul's request to see the Jews and in his reminder to Timothy; the sense is the ground or cause.
In Act 28:18 the noun stands in a legal setting, where the Romans found no ground for the death penalty after examining Paul; the lexicon lists the legal sense 'charge, case, ground for accusation'.

senses.obs_text: In Mat 17:25, 18:12, 21:28, 22:17, 22:42, Luk 10:36, Joh 11:56 and Heb 10:29 the present verb 'to think' stands in a question that asks the hearer for his opinion: what do you think, which of these three do you think; the sense is 'to hold an opinion', asked for.

In Mat 6:7, 26:53, Luk 12:51, 13:2, 13:4, Joh 5:39, Joh 5:45 and Joh 16:2 the verb 'to think' states a supposition or assumption about a state of affairs, often one the verse corrects: that many words will be heard, that Jesus cannot appeal, that he came to give peace; the sense is 'to suppose'.

In 1Cor 4:9, 1Cor 7:40, 1Cor 12:23 and 2Cor 11:16 the verb 'to think' states the speaker's own judgment or esteem (I think God has exhibited us, we think less honorable, let no one think me foolish); the sense is 'to judge, deem', an estimate of persons or parts.
